points.t: Any **dry or eczematous skin**, at every review, alongside active treatment.
They replace lipids and water in the stratum corneum, restore the barrier and reduce itch and flares.
The right emollient is **the one they’ll use**: children **250–500 g / week**, also as a soap substitute.
**Fire risk** with any emollient soaked into fabrics (MHRA); slips; stinging from aqueous cream.

points: **Humectants** (urea, glycerol, lactic acid) draw water in.
**Emollient lipids** (ceramides, oils) fill gaps in the barrier.
They reduce irritant and allergen penetration and itch, and are **steroid-sparing**.

visuals.caption: Emollients restore the lipid ‘mortar’ between skin cells, so less water escapes and fewer irritants get in.

features.lead: Lotion → cream → gel → ointment: greasier works better and has fewer preservatives.
points: Use as **leave-on** treatment and as a **soap substitute**; bath additives rarely.
Fit to dryness, site, time of day, school or work, preference.
Offer **2–4 to try**; prescribe enough for **home and school** (NICE CG57).

visuals.caption: From light to greasy: lotion, cream, gel and ointment. Greasier products hold water in best and contain the least preservative; lighter ones suit daytime and hairy areas.
visuals.alt: Four emollient containers from light to greasy

points: **250–500 g / week** for children; **~500 g / week** for adults with widespread dryness.
One 500 g tub every 3 months = under-using.
Worse with a product: suspect contact allergy; patch test.

cards.name: Aqueous cream BP
cards.clue: **Not** a leave-on: SLS stings and damages the barrier (MHRA 2013).

cards.name: Colloidal oatmeal cream
cards.clue: Leave-on; rare oat allergy; check formulary.

cards.name: Greasy ointments
cards.clue: Leave-on and soap substitute; **high fire risk** on fabric.

cards.name: Emulsifying ointment
cards.clue: Leave-on and wash; older versions had SLS: switch if it stings.

manage.lead: Emollients are the treatment, not an extra.

points: **Pump dispensers**; separate tub for soap substitute.
Smooth on **in the direction of hair growth** (less folliculitis).
At least **2–4 times daily** and after washing, even when clear.
Leave a gap between emollient and steroid.
**Fire risk** with paraffin and paraffin-free emollients on clothing, bedding, dressings: no smoking or naked flames; tell carers.
**Slips** with bath additives; BATHE trial: no added benefit.

visuals.caption: Smooth emollient on in long strokes along the direction of hair growth; rubbing hard against it can block follicles and cause folliculitis.
visuals.alt: Hand applying cream along the forearm

limits.t: Residue on fabric burns easily; washing may not remove it.

items.t: Uncontrolled despite adequate emollient + TCS: refer per NICE CG57.
Suspected emollient contact allergy: patch testing.
Erythroderma or infected eczema: assess promptly.

pearls.t: Show the FTU **and** a handful of emollient: a 500 g tub lasts about a week in widespread childhood eczema.
Fire-safety counselling is an MHRA expectation: record it.
Fully within IP and OTC scope; follow ICB self-care policy.

quiz.q: Weekly emollient for a child with eczema (NICE)?
Why not aqueous cream as a leave-on?
quiz.a: Contains SLS: stinging and barrier damage (MHRA 2013).
In the direction of hair growth, to reduce folliculitis.

quiz.q: Fire risk applies to which emollients?
quiz.a: Both paraffin-containing and paraffin-free products soaked into fabric.
